title: Fatayer with Spinach
subtitle: Lebanese spinach pastries baked in the oven
excerpt: Small triangular pastries filled with spinach, sumac, and pine nuts. The yeasted dough is light and the filling is tangy and slightly sour. They are popular across Lebanon and Syria as a snack or starter.
sourceNotes: Fatayer are baked pastries eaten across the Levant. The spinach version is one of the most common. They are popular as a breakfast food, as part of mezze, and as a street snack in Lebanon and Syria.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked and cooled fatayer. Reheat in a 180C oven for 10 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Shape and refrigerate unbaked. Bake the next day.

content.text: Squeeze the spinach very dry before using it. Wet filling makes the pastry base soggy and the fatayer will not hold their shape. The corners of the triangle need to be pinched very firmly so they do not open during baking.

items.prepNote: use 1 tsp sumac -- or extra lemon juice

content.text: Mix the yeast with 200ml warm water. Leave for 5 minutes until frothy.
Mix the flour, salt, and olive oil in a bowl. Pour in the yeast mixture. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth. Cover and leave for 1 hour until doubled.
Make the filling: mix the squeezed spinach, diced onion, lemon juice, sumac, pine nuts, and olive oil. Season with salt.
Preheat oven to 200C (fan 180C / gas 6). Line two baking sheets with baking paper.
Divide the dough into 12 balls. Roll each into a 12cm circle.
Place a spoonful of filling in the centre. Bring three sides up and pinch firmly together to form a triangle. Seal every corner tightly.
Place on the baking sheets. Brush lightly with olive oil. Bake for 18 to 20 minutes until golden.

items.cause: Corners not sealed firmly or filling too wet
items.fix: Squeeze the spinach very dry. Pinch the corners firmly -- dampen the dough edges slightly before sealing.
Leave the dough in a warm place until it has clearly doubled. Do not rush the proof.

items.symptom: Filling leaks and burns on the tray
items.fix: Use less filling than you think you need. A tablespoon per fatayer is enough.

content.text: Fatayer are popular street food and home-baked snacks across Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, and Jordan. The spinach version, with sumac for sourness and pine nuts for richness, is one of the most common. They are a fixture at Lebanese bakeries, at family picnics, and as part of a mezze spread. The dough is the same used for many other flat breads in the region.
